id_and_class.summary: Bitar explains consciousness through the structure of the mind, which he calls the automatic-volitional architecture. A parallel automatic unit handles many sensory inputs and motor outputs at once, unconsciously, while a serial volitional unit manages the body under direct intentional control, and consciousness is the subjective concept we use for information as the serial unit represents it. Mental activity seems immaterial only because it is private, so Bitar treats it as material and considers the mind-body problem solved.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as Serially Represented Information in the Mind’s Volitional Unit

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is the subjective concept we use to characterize information as represented by the volitional unit, the mind’s high-level serial processing unit. Bitar calls this serial format the objective definition of consciousness.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: The mind is the control system of an animal and is implemented by its brain. Mental activity is material but private, and Bitar compares rejecting its immateriality to biology’s rejection of vitalism.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Weak emergence (consciousness follows from the serial organization of the brain’s control system)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Subjectivity reflects the privacy of mental activity, which our senses cannot observe directly. Volitional processes are directly intentional, and automatic processes are not.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Experiences are material states that only seem immaterial because they are private. Bitar imagines a brain that displayed visual experience on a screen on the back of the head, arguing that if this were how brains worked, nobody would think experience immaterial.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Brains, goal-processing control systems, and four functional components: a sensory unit, a motor unit, a parallel automatic unit, and a serial volitional unit.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Each person observes only their own mind and infers other minds from similarity of bodily structure and function and from behavior.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: A sensory unit, a motor unit, an automatic parallel-processing unit (the ‘engine’), and a volitional serial-processing unit (the ‘pilot’).

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Volition, attention, and conscious versus unconscious processing; the mind-body problem
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Conscious processes are necessarily serial and unconscious processes run in parallel. The volitional unit focuses attention and approves or rejects proposals from the automatic unit, which executes the approved ones.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: The prefrontal cortex plays a major role in the volitional unit through executive functions, while most of the rest of the brain implements the automatic unit. Bitar notes that the cerebral components of both units have not been identified.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: The volitional unit centrally manages the body, while the automatic unit maximizes the body’s response rate. Bitar argues an animal without either could not survive.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Information is represented in parallel form in the automatic unit and in serial form in the volitional unit, and only the serial representation is conscious.
mechanism_and_dynamics.evolutionary_account: The automatic-volitional architecture is necessary for survival, which Bitar takes to explain why animals with brains have it.
core_claims_and_evidence: Survival requires a parallel unit for fast response and a serial unit for central management of the body.
Volitional processes are conscious and serial, and automatic processes are unconscious and parallel.
Assuming mental activity is immaterial adds needless complexity, since it raises the question of how a material brain causes immaterial activity.
Bitar argues that Chalmers’s 1996 argument that consciousness is not physical assumes what it sets out to prove.
A theory should be judged first by predictive accuracy, then by simplicity, with logical coherence assumed.

empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: The cerebral regions implementing the volitional and automatic units have not been identified, and Bitar presumes they are largely distinct but overlap at their boundaries.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent with materialism and with Bitar’s goal of matching mainstream science. Defining consciousness by an architecture sits uneasily with denying consciousness to a robot that has the same architecture, which Bitar resolves by appeal to simplicity.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Bitar argues that even a robot with an automatic-volitional architecture and humanlike behavior gives no rationale for attributing consciousness, because we know only that biological representation of information yields experience.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since the mind is implemented by the brain and mental activity is material, it follows from the view that the mind ends with the brain.

virtual_immortality.rationale: Bitar withholds consciousness from electronic systems, so an electronic copy of a mind would not, on his view, be credited with experience.

related_theories.name: Baars's and Dehaene's Global Workspace Theory

sources_and_references.title_with_names: Why Human Life Makes Sense, Edition 5, Philip Bitar
